scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Country dances originated in England and entered Continental courtly awareness in the late seventeenth century.
The genre was introduced to the French court of Louis XIV in 1684 under the name anglaise.
André Lorin visited the English court in the late seventeenth century and presented Louis XIV with a manuscript of dances in the English style upon his return.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance was conceived for broad social participation rather than solo spectacle.
By allowing dancers to progress through the set and encounter every other couple, it created an egalitarian, interactive social atmosphere within structured ballroom etiquette.
Today it is a revived tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Angloise is executed by sets of dancers who carry out predefined sequences of figures repeated over the course of a tune.
Most commonly arranged in longways sets—two facing lines of partners—or four-couple squares, dancers progress through the set to interact with each couple.
Figures trace circular, serpentine, angular, and straight lines on the floor, including simple communal movements like Circle Left and complex progressive figures such as Strip the Willow.
Watch for Circle Left, Strip the Willow.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for the dance is structured in fixed lengths to match the choreographic figures, most commonly 32-bar jigs or reels composed in 2/4 or 6/8 meter.
Traditional, folk, and historical instrumental ensembles accompanied the dance.
The pulse is 2/4 or 6/8.

Bright and rhythmic dance music organized into repeating strains, usually composed in 2/4 or 6/8 time. Designed to fit the length of dance figures, it commonly uses 32-bar structures characteristic of jigs and reels.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Originally performed in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century European aristocratic courts and formal ballrooms, the dance functioned as a refreshing, energetic finale to social evenings dominated by stately dances such as the minuet.
Historical clothing reflected court and ballroom attire of the eighteenth century.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historical figures include King Louis XIV of France, who welcomed the dance to his court in 1684; André Lorin, who presented an English dance manuscript to the French monarch; Raoul Auger Feuillet, who published the 1706 notation manual Recüeil de Contredances; John Essex, who translated Feuillet's work into English; dance writer Thomas Wilson (1808, 1820); and classical composers Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and Ludwig van Beethoven.

Variants of the dance include the French contredanse, the Scandinavian Engelska (or Danish Engelsk, a 16-bar folk dance in 2/4), the Scottish écossaise, Irish set dance, New England contra dance, and the Spanish and Latin American contradanza.
Emanating from English country dances documented in works such as John Playford's 1651 The English Dancing Master, the Angloise synthesized British country figures with French court dance.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Angloise is parent of English country dance: The Angloise derived directly from the English country dance traditions popularized by John Playford.
Angloise is variant of Contredanse: The French court's adaptation of the English country dance.
Angloise is child of Quadrille: Developed out of eighteenth-century French square-set contredanses.
Angloise is child of Contradanza: The Spanish and Latin American descendant of the French contredanse.
